title: A read-only window into my lab for AI agents
summary: I gave my coding agents a typed, read-only view of my homelab over MCP, added a one-call overview, and let an independent review agent catch me widening what they could read.

stat.label: every tool is a typed read that fails loudly, and a test refuses anything outside its allowlist

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: My coding agents work in the cloud and cannot reach my home network. Before this, every question about live state went through me, pasting a command into a session on the LAN. A general shell tool would have fixed that and handed an agent far more power than it needs.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A Model Context Protocol server that exposes the lab as a small set of typed, read-only tools: host lookups, guest state, monitor status, git history, service health, and work-item lookups. A model calls a tool with validated input and gets a capped answer that names what it read.

It acts alone on reads only. It needs my word for anything that runs code from a branch, so that stays a separate, later design. It never writes, never returns a secret value, and has no shell tool. A read that fails returns an error with the cause, never an empty success.

The upgrade in this study makes the work-item tools project-aware. A tool takes a key such as one from the infrastructure board or the portfolio board. The server finds the project itself, so an agent no longer needs a hand-fed project identifier. A second tool lists the projects it may read.

A second upgrade cut round trips. Asking what is wrong used to take four calls: monitors, guests, the merge desk and the services. One overview tool now runs those four reads together and returns a short list of what needs a look. Each source succeeds or fails on its own, and a source that cannot be read is named in the list. An unreadable source never counts as healthy, and the call fails outright only when every source fails.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: Agents can name the work items a commit cites, across boards, in one call. I have no measurement of time saved, and I am not claiming one. What I can show is the control below.

sections.heading: What went wrong
paragraphs: My first version resolved any project in the workspace. The tests passed. I handed the diff to a fresh review agent with no stake in it, and told it nothing about whether the change was safe. It pointed out that I had removed a hard limit. Before, the tool could read one board. Now a model, or text a model had been tricked by, could ask for any board, including one I treat as personal.
I had tested that the code worked and never asked what it could now reach. I added an allowlist of project identifiers, checked before the server contacts the tracker at all.

sections.heading: The tested control
paragraphs: The limit is the allowlist, and tests cover both sides. A key from an allowed board resolves and returns its title and state. A key from a board outside the list is refused, and the test asserts that no work-item request left the server. The refusal means something because the allowed case succeeds beside it. Other tests fail a call when the token is refused, when a project list is empty, and when an item belongs to a different project than its key claims.

The overview has its own negative cases. A dead source shows up as unread, a desk that stopped without raising an error is flagged by its silence, and a source that answers in the wrong shape is reported by name instead of crashing the view. An independent review agent found the silent-desk gap; the same pattern, a check that stays green because it stopped working, is what the review exists to catch.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: When a change makes a tool more general, review what it can now reach, not only whether it works. Ask an independent reviewer that question, and write the refusal as a test.

sources: the lab MCP server's tests and review notes
